summary.en: Sixteen great realms (mahajanapadas) arise across the Indo-Gangetic plain as iron tools, rice farming and walled cities spread. Magadha, Kosala, Avanti and Vatsa compete for supremacy while Buddhism and Jainism emerge. The northwest passes to the Achaemenid Persians around 518 BCE.

summary.en: Magadha under the Nandas swallows its neighbours and builds the first great empire of the Gangetic plain, with a vast army and treasury. In the northwest, Alexander of Macedon crosses the Indus in 327–325 BCE but his soldiers refuse to march further east.

summary.en: Chandragupta Maurya, guided by Kautilya, overthrows the Nandas, drives out Macedonian garrisons and unites north India. His successor Bindusara extends the empire south into the Deccan.

summary.en: After the bloody conquest of Kalinga, Ashoka embraces Buddhist ideals of dhamma and carves his edicts on rocks and pillars across the subcontinent. The Maurya state is the largest in Indian history until the Mughals, covering nearly all except the far south.

summary.en: The Maurya empire fragments. Shungas hold the Gangetic heartland, Indo-Greeks rule the northwest, the Satavahanas build power in the Deccan and Kharavela’s Kalinga flourishes. Tamil kingdoms trade pepper and pearls with Rome.

summary.en: The Kushan empire links the Silk Road with the Gangetic plain under Kanishka, patronising Gandharan art and Mahayana Buddhism. The Satavahanas dominate the Deccan and Roman gold flows into southern ports.

summary.en: The Guptas unite much of north India. Mathematics (zero and the decimal system), astronomy, Sanskrit literature and temple building flourish; Nalanda is founded. The Chinese monk Faxian visits around 405 CE.

summary.en: After the Guptas, Harsha of Kannauj briefly reunites the north. The Chalukyas of Badami check him on the Narmada and the Pallavas build great temples at Mamallapuram. Xuanzang studies at Nalanda (637–642). In 712 Arab forces take Sindh.

summary.en: Three powers fight for Kannauj and the Gangetic plain: the Gurjara-Pratiharas from the west, the Palas from Bengal and Bihar, and the Rashtrakutas from the Deccan. Adi Shankara’s philosophy spreads across the land and Nalanda and Vikramashila prosper under the Palas.

summary.en: The Cholas under Rajaraja and Rajendra command the Bay of Bengal, conquering Lanka and sending a fleet to Southeast Asia. In the northwest Mahmud of Ghazni raids deep into India and annexes the Punjab. Regional Rajput and Kalachuri houses rule the north.
summary.hi: The Cholas under Rajaraja and Rajendra command the Bay of Bengal, conquering Lanka and sending a fleet to Southeast Asia. In the northwest Mahmud of Ghazni raids deep into India and annexes the Punjab. Regional Rajput and Kalachuri houses rule the north.

summary.en: Qutb-ud-din Aibak founds the Delhi Sultanate in 1206. Within a generation it reaches from the Indus to Bengal. Nalanda and Vikramashila decline; Persian, Turkic and Indian cultures begin to blend in language, music and architecture. Mongol armies threaten the northwest.

title.hi: तुग़लक़ साम्राज्य और दक्षिण का उत्थान

summary.en: Under Muhammad bin Tughlaq the Delhi Sultanate reaches its greatest extent, even moving the capital to Daulatabad. Overstretched, it soon loses the Deccan and the south. In 1336 Harihara and Bukka found Vijayanagara on the Tungabhadra. Ibn Battuta serves at Delhi (1334–41).
summary.hi: Under Muhammad bin Tughlaq the Delhi Sultanate reaches its greatest extent, even moving the capital to Daulatabad. Overstretched, it soon loses the Deccan and the south. In 1336 Harihara and Bukka found Vijayanagara on the Tungabhadra. Ibn Battuta serves at Delhi (1334–41).

summary.en: India divides into powerful regional states. Vijayanagara dominates the south, the Bahmani sultanate splits into five Deccan sultanates, Gujarat and Bengal are rich trading sultanates, and the Lodis hold Delhi. Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut in 1498; Babur wins Panipat in 1526 and Vijayanagara falls at Talikota in 1565.
summary.hi: India divides into powerful regional states. Vijayanagara dominates the south, the Bahmani sultanate splits into five Deccan sultanates, Gujarat and Bengal are rich trading sultanates, and the Lodis hold Delhi. Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut in 1498; Babur wins Panipat in 1526 and Vijayanagara falls at Talikota in 1565.

summary.en: Akbar builds a centralised empire with a revenue system (mansabdari), religious tolerance and a brilliant Indo-Persian court at Agra and Fatehpur Sikri. Jahangir and Shah Jahan later commission the great monuments, including the Taj Mahal.
summary.hi: Akbar builds a centralised empire with a revenue system (mansabdari), religious tolerance and a brilliant Indo-Persian court at Agra and Fatehpur Sikri. Jahangir and Shah Jahan later commission the great monuments, including the Taj Mahal.

note.en: Capitals at Agra, Fatehpur Sikri and Lahore.
note.hi: Capitals at Agra, Fatehpur Sikri and Lahore.

summary.en: Aurangzeb extends the Mughal empire to its largest extent but is drawn into a quarter-century of war in the Deccan against the Marathas, whose Swarajya was founded by Shivaji (crowned 1674). The empire is overstretched and begins to unravel after his death in 1707.
summary.hi: Aurangzeb extends the Mughal empire to its largest extent but is drawn into a quarter-century of war in the Deccan against the Marathas, whose Swarajya was founded by Shivaji (crowned 1674). The empire is overstretched and begins to unravel after his death in 1707.

summary.en: As Mughal power collapses, successor states emerge: the Nizam in Hyderabad, the Nawabs of Awadh and Bengal, the Sikh misls, and the Maratha Confederacy under the Peshwas, which reaches its widest extent by 1760 before defeat at Panipat (1761). Meanwhile the East India Company wins at Plassey (1757).

summary.en: After the Third Anglo-Maratha War the East India Company is paramount. Punjab (1849), Sindh and Awadh (1856) are annexed. The Uprising of 1857 shakes Company rule; in 1858 the Crown assumes control. About a third of the land stays under hundreds of princely states.

note.en: Presidencies of Bengal, Bombay and Madras.

summary.en: On 14–15 August 1947 British rule ends and two dominions, India and Pakistan, are created. Partition of Punjab and Bengal triggers one of history’s largest migrations, with great loss of life. Over 560 princely states are integrated over the next years; the status of Jammu & Kashmir remains disputed.
